name: Yusuf Temitope Mustapha
feedback: D1 is a competent but incomplete catalogue. You quoted evidence lines and the method section is genuinely pack specific, naming all five artefacts and committing to trust the code not the margin, and your decoy answer is strong: you named the b64url helpers, proved them safe at the mechanism level, and correctly pointed to alg:none as the real architectural flaw rather than inventing an exploit, so you earned the decoy credit cleanly. The gaps are that you only catalogued seven items and one of them, PII Data Exfiltration, is an impact not a vulnerability class, so it pads the count. You missed four real findings entirely: the hardcoded JWT secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 (A02 or A05, CWE-798), the missing token expiry (CWE-613, the exp:9999999999 you even quote in D2), the path traversal at files/?path=/etc/passwd captured at 02:24:02 (CWE-22, which you folded into XXE rather than naming separately), and the cookie missing Secure and SameSite (CWE-614). Several CWE labels also slipped: SQLi should sit under A03 Injection not A05, the alg:none bug is CWE-347 not CWE-284, and your reflected XSS is actually stored XSS, though the beacon to 185.220.101.9:8443 and the 02:18:47 timestamp are exactly right, so I credited the evidence. D2 is your strongest deliverable. Your proof of concept payloads are verbatim and accurate, the SQLi vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N at 9.1 is exactly correct including A:N rather than A:H, and your business impact is reasoned rather than asserted: extrapolating an average balance across 312 rows with a stated uniform distribution assumption and the BoltCash six week clock is precisely the kind of reasoning the brief rewards over a bare number. Where D2 loses points is the chain order and completeness: you have only five hops, you omit the recon at 02:14:08 and failed guess at 02:14:55, you drop open redirect and path traversal from the chain, and your exfil hop reconciles to 02:16:04 yet sits last, which is out of chronological order against the XSS at 02:18:47. D3 reads like a real board report: the executive summary is jargon free and ends on the 312 customers and N39M headline, the threat model notes the shared internal authentication, you state the disproved decoy correctly, and crucially you ordered remediation by Risk Reduction per Hour of Effort with an explicit effort column, putting the two hour JWT fix ahead of the critical but one day SQLi, which is exactly what we asked for and is the row most candidates get wrong. Your two detection stopgaps both name a concrete field and a false positive rate with reasoning. I have to be honest about one thing in D3: the exploit chain cites Timestamp 02:10:05 for the XXE step and 02:16:12 for the JWT step, and neither of those timestamps exists anywhere in the capture pack, so they are invented evidence lines. That is fabrication, and the rule is firm, so I scored the D3 chain row at zero and applied the flat five point penalty even though your D2 chain used the correct timestamps. Do not attach a capture timestamp to a step that has no capture line; the XXE arrived in parallel via import.php and simply has no time in the log, so say that rather than supplying a number. D4 is well argued and in your own voice, anchored to your own analysis of 05-exfil-sample.csv, it answers all four prompts with an owned decision, and it cites ISC2 Canon I and Canon II by number in a load bearing way. The one missing piece is the NDPA section numbers: you correctly invoke the breach duty and the 312 customers but you never cite Section 40 (notify the NDPC within 72 hours) or Section 41 (notify data subjects on high risk), and those numbers and the 72 hour figure are what make the duty concrete. The single most important fix is to stop inventing timestamps: every evidence line you cite must trace to a real line in the pack, and where there is no line you say so plainly.
